How the statistics and the calorie and protein recommendations are calculated, with the exact formulas and the references they are based on.

«Current weight» is your latest weigh-in in the period. «Trend» is the most recent value of the 7-day moving average. «Change» compares the first and last weigh-ins of the selected period, and «rate» is the slope of the regression described below.

All your entries dated within the 7-day window ending on d are averaged. Days without entries are neither counted nor filled with zeros: if you only weighed yourself 3 times that week, the average is of those 3 entries. This smooths out daily noise (water, salt, gut content) and reveals the real trend, which changes slowly. Regular self-weighing is associated with more weight loss and with no negative psychological effects (Zheng et al. 2015); the average turns those weigh-ins into a trend that does not jump with each day\'s number. The Hacker\'s Diet popularised the same «trend weight» idea, though with an exponential moving average; here a simple 7-day average is used, which is easier to interpret.

x is the number of days since the first entry in the range and y the recorded weight. The slope β is multiplied by 7 to express it per week. The regression uses your raw entries in the visible range: it captures the long-term direction better than comparing just two points.
Daily calories, protein, carbs and fat

Each day\'s total is the sum of that day\'s meals (calories, protein, carbs and fat are computed when saving, by adding up the ingredients or taking your manual total). The chart shows the logged days with the same 7-day moving average and, if your profile is complete, the band of your calorie target. «Macro average» is the mean of the days with meals logged: unlogged days do not count, because counting them as 0 would say you ate less than you did; «Days logged: N of M» tells how complete the data is. The calorie split uses 4 kcal per gram of protein and carbs and 9 kcal per gram of fat.

Protein is calculated by multiplying a g/kg factor, which depends on your goal, by your latest logged weight. The big number is the middle of the range.

Maintain: 1.4–2.0 g/kg, the range of the ISSN position stand for people who train (Jäger et al. 2017). Bulk: 1.6–2.2 g/kg. The meta-analysis by Morton et al. (2018) puts the point beyond which the benefit for muscle mass stops growing at ~1.6 g/kg, with a confidence interval reaching 2.2 g/kg, which is the range Iraki et al. (2019) recommend for bulking. Cut: 1.8–2.7 g/kg. A deficit needs more protein to preserve muscle; this range roughly matches the 2.3–3.1 g/kg of lean mass recommended in a deficit (Helms et al. 2014, IJSNEM; Jäger et al. 2017) for a typical body fat percentage.

If you are cutting and have logged your body fat at some weigh-in, the app uses the most recent value to calculate your lean mass (weight × (1 − body fat %)) and applies 2.3–3.1 g/kg to it. This is more accurate: fat tissue barely raises protein needs, so a total-body-weight factor overshoots for people with more fat and falls short for very lean ones. Maintain and bulk use total body weight, which is how the studies express those ranges. In adults with overweight or obesity, more than 1.3 g/kg of body weight already helps preserve muscle mass during weight loss, although in that meta-analysis it did not improve strength or physical function (Kokura et al. 2024), and in general more protein supports lean mass, especially together with strength training (Nunes et al. 2022).

If your BMI is above 25, the ranges apply to the weight you would have at BMI 25 (25 × height²) instead of your actual weight, as clinical nutrition does (McClave et al. 2016): the studies behind these ranges are mostly in normal-weight people, and fat tissue barely raises protein needs. For example, 110 kg at 1.80 m uses 81 kg; a cut gives 146–219 g/day (1.3–2.0 g/kg of actual weight), in line with the more than 1.3 g/kg of Kokura et al. (2024). If you have logged a body fat below the one that goes with BMI 25 for your sex and age (Gallagher et al. 2000: for men 20% up to 39 years, 22% from 40 to 59 and 25% from 60; for women 33%, 34% and 36%), the high BMI is muscle and your actual weight is used. When cutting with body fat logged, lean mass is still used.
gym = gym days × minutes per session / 7 [min/day]

Total expenditure is estimated in two steps. First, the basal metabolic rate (BMR) with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation (1990), the most reliable one in healthy adults with and without obesity according to the systematic review by Frankenfield et al. (2005). Then it is multiplied by your physical activity level (PAL), which the app calculates from what you do instead of asking you to pick a category.

This is the factorial method of FAO/WHO/UNU (2004): the 1440 minutes of the day are split into blocks and each counts by its intensity, as a multiple of BMR. Minutes without exercise (sleeping, sitting, light chores) count 1.4, the low end of the «sedentary or light» band (PAL 1.40–1.69). The gym counts 4.0: the 2024 Compendium of Physical Activities gives resistance training 3.5–6 METs, and a real session includes rest between sets. Walking counts 3.5 (moderate pace, 4–5 km/h). METs are used as multiples of your BMR: an approximation, because 1 MET (3.5 ml O₂/kg/min) is usually somewhat above the real resting metabolic rate (Byrne et al. 2005), so exercise energy comes out on the low side, in line with a conservative model. For example, 3 sessions of 60 minutes a week and 30 minutes of walking a day give a PAL of 1.49; no exercise, 1.40.

Why not an activity scale? Many apps ask you to pick your level (from sedentary to very active). What people report about their activity often differs from what is measured and, against accelerometers, it is usually higher, especially for vigorous activity (Prince et al. 2008). Here you only give times (days, minutes of gym and of walking) and the app sets the intensity with cautious values, so you do not have to judge whether you are «active» or «very active»; and every extra minute of exercise raises the result smoothly, without jumps between categories. The model is deliberately conservative and does not include other activity (physical work, sports); if your days are more active, the measured expenditure will show it.

The goal adds or subtracts a fixed amount from the TDEE: cut −400 kcal (range −500 to −300), maintain ±100 kcal, bulk +300 kcal (range +200 to +400). Using the approximation of ~7700 kcal per kg (Hall 2008), −400 kcal/day is about 0.36 kg/week, a prudent pace: Helms et al. (2014, JISSN) recommend losing 0.5–1% of body weight per week to preserve muscle (0.35–0.7 kg at 70 kg). +300 kcal/day is about 0.27 kg/week, in line with the 0.25–0.5% per week that Iraki et al. (2019) suggest for bulking. The range never goes below your BMR: if the deficit would take it lower (small, not very active people), it stays at the BMR; a deeper deficit is best done under supervision.

The formula is a population estimate: two people with the same data can burn several hundred kcal apart. When there is enough data, the app measures your real expenditure from what you eat and how your weight changes, as adaptive apps such as MacroFactor do: if your weight holds steady, you burn what you eat; if it goes up or down, the difference is the energy you store or lose.
intake = mean kcal of the days with meals logged
β = slope of the weight regression [kg/day]

Today does not count, because you are still logging it. Days without meals are left out: counting them as 0 kcal would make you look like you burn far less. Even so, your weight also reflects what you ate on those days, so at least 21 logged days out of 28 are required (3 out of every 4).

A weigh-in can vary ±0.5–1 kg from one day to the next because of water, salt or glycogen, and half a kilo of error in a 4-week trend is more than 100 kcal/day. That is why the app calculates the statistical margin of error of the slope. σ is the scatter of your weigh-ins around the trend line, never less than 0.5 kg, so that a few weigh-ins that happen to line up do not look precise. Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² grows with the number of weigh-ins and how spread out they are. If you weigh yourself several times on one day, that day counts once, as the mean: two weigh-ins on the same day are not two independent measurements of the trend. The measured expenditure is only shown, with its 95% ±, when the margin is ±300 kcal/day or less and there are at least 4 weigh-in days spanning 14 days or more. In practice: weighing yourself once a week never gets there; about 3 times a week does; daily, the margin drops to about ±180 kcal.

It does not replace your goal: the recommended range still comes from the formula, so that it does not swing with scale noise. Use it as a cross-check: if it differs from the estimated TDEE for several weeks, it is the best reference for your real expenditure. Its accuracy depends on logging meals accurately (if you under-log, expenditure will look lower), and when you start or change a diet, shifts in water and glycogen can distort it for the first weeks. The 7700 kcal/kg is also an approximation: the real value depends on how much of what is gained or lost is fat and how much lean tissue (Hall 2008).

Photos and text («3 bananas») become foods, grams and macros with a language model: the provider you choose in Settings → AI, or the model on your phone. It is an estimate: the model does not weigh the food, it judges it from the photo, the size references (plate, cutlery, your hand), the nutrition label if you photograph it and what you describe.

The app asks for a fixed answer format, checks that it has valid foods and macros and always opens the review form before saving: nothing the AI says is logged unless you confirm it. On-device models are smaller than cloud ones and make more mistakes.

The coach uses the numbers the app computes (your targets, measured expenditure and weight projection) instead of working out its own. The 30-day projection extends the trend line of the last 4 weeks with its 95 % margin; it does not account for future changes in your diet. It is not medical advice.

Generic foods (offline): Swiss Food Composition Database of the Swiss Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office (FSVO) and the Ciqual 2020 table by Anses (France, Licence Ouverte / Etalab 2.0). Spanish names are added by this project.\n\nProducts and barcodes: Open Food Facts, an open database under the Open Database License (ODbL). Each product\'s data comes from its contributors and may contain errors. Values are per 100 g of the food as described by the source.
